dailyBrief.text: Tough morning, Cleveland: the Guardians' season ended last night in St. Petersburg, a 7-3 loss to Tampa Bay in ALCS Game 6 that sends the Rays to the World Series instead. Overnight, Zelenskiy arrived in Oslo for talks with U.S. envoy Witkoff and European leaders on ending the war, even as a Russian drone killed three people on the highway south of Kyiv. Closer to home, Nestlé confirmed it will close its Solon factory by the end of 2027 and move production to South Carolina — the campus stays, and the city is promising job help for affected workers. Solon woke up clear and cold at 37°, but it's a sunny, dry day ahead with a high near 68°. Today in town: the CLEO on the Go Luncheon at Mavis Public House at 11:30, and the Browns get a quiet week to enjoy first place before Sunday at Tennessee.

weekBrief.text: It's a crisp, dry fall week in Solon: sunny skies almost every day, highs in the mid-to-upper 60s and chilly nights in the 30s and 40s, with today topping out near 68°. The Guardians' October run is over after Monday's Game 6 loss, so the sports baton passes on: the Cavs open Thursday night at Philadelphia and play their home opener Saturday against Brooklyn, and the first-place Browns head to Tennessee on Sunday. Around town it's a full week — trunk-or-treat Thursday in Solon, Heinen's clam bake Friday in Chagrin Falls, and Barack Obama rallying in Cleveland on Saturday for the fall races, while Solon digests the news that Nestlé will wind down its factory here by the end of 2027. Grocery play of the week is still Giant Eagle's free-turkey deal — spend $350 by November 8 — and with the baby countdown very much on, it's a good week to knock a few more checklist items off together.

Zelenskiy arrives in Oslo for talks as U.S. envoy Witkoff joins the push to end the war
items.summary:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy arrived in Oslo on Tuesday for talks on the war and European security, hosted by Norway with Finland taking part. U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff was expected at the meetings, along with representatives from Britain, France, Germany and Poland and officials from the EU and NATO.

The meeting comes at a strained moment between Kyiv and Washington. President Trump has waived some sanctions on Russia, praised Moscow's conduct and said Ukraine should find somebody else to negotiate, while Kyiv says it has lately missed early warnings of Russian missile launches, seen its Starshield satellite links throttled and waited on air defenses its European allies already paid for.

That is why Oslo matters beyond the photo opportunity. If the U.S. envoy, the Europeans and Zelenskiy leave with a shared position, the peace track still has a shape. If they do not, Ukraine faces a winter of heavier Russian strikes with cooler support from its most important partner.

Watch for the joint press conference with Zelenskiy, Finland's President Alexander Stubb and Norway's Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Stoere later Tuesday.

items.title: Russian drone strike near a highway south of Kyiv kills three people
items.summary:
A Russian drone struck near a petrol station on the highway running south from Kyiv toward the Black Sea port of Odesa on Tuesday, killing three people, according to the Kyiv regional prosecutor's office. Several cars caught fire and four more people were wounded.

Ukrainian emergency services released footage of firefighters working through twisted wreckage in the dark. The strike is part of a pattern both sides have settled into: Russia hitting Ukrainian cities, energy systems and transport routes while Ukraine targets Russian energy infrastructure in return.

Civilian road traffic has become part of the risk map in Ukraine, not just front-line towns. Each strike like this also hardens Kyiv's argument in Oslo and Washington that air defense deliveries are the difference between intercepted drones and funerals.

items.title: Kremlin says it hopes Witkoff can brief Putin soon after the Oslo talks
items.summary:
The Kremlin said Tuesday it hopes a meeting in Russia between President Vladimir Putin and U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff can be arranged in the near future. Spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Witkoff could brief Putin on what he hears from the Ukrainians and Europeans in Oslo.

Peskov called such meetings timely and substantive and praised the American mediation effort. Some U.S. media have reported Witkoff could meet Putin as early as Wednesday in St. Petersburg, though Moscow gave no date.

The comment shows Moscow wants to stay inside the negotiating loop even as its forces step up attacks. A recent Trump-Putin call produced a Russian diesel supply agreement that Trump said could lower U.S. fuel prices, a deal that alarmed Ukraine and its European allies.

Watch whether a Witkoff-Putin meeting is confirmed, and whether it produces anything more concrete than another round of statements.

items.title: Attack on an Australian lawmaker follows years of rising threats to public figures
items.summary:
An Australian independent lawmaker, Helen Haines, was seriously injured Monday when a man rammed a car into her outside her electorate office in Wangaratta, about 150 miles from Melbourne. Media and officials said she lost a leg, with doctors working to save the other, and police have not yet stated a motive.

The attack landed in a country already debating how toxic its political conversation has become. Health Minister Mark Butler said Australians have seen a level of hate and intolerance in public debate that the country did not used to see, and opposition figures echoed that threats against lawmakers are increasing, not decreasing.

A 2025 parliamentary report found as many as 85% of federal lawmakers and their staff had experienced violent, threatening or volatile behavior, with incidents reported more than once a month by nearly half of respondents. Australian politicians traditionally live in their communities with minimal security and easy public access.

The case now tests whether that open style can survive, and what new security arrangements Parliament puts in place.

items.title: Giant 'heat storms' are reshaping weather around the world, a Reuters investigation finds
items.summary:
This decade, so-called heat storms have swarmed the planet at an average of about 102 a year, according to a Reuters examination of the phenomenon. One of them drove this summer's deadly heat in Europe, producing the highest June temperatures ever recorded in Bordeaux, Budapest and Bilbao, where it reached 108.9 degrees.

Governments estimated more than 10,000 excess deaths in a single week during that European event, as heat warped steel railroad tracks and zookeepers fed tigers meat frozen in ice. The largest heat storm on record lasted 367 days across 2023 and 2024 and at its reach covered almost 85% of the globe.

The same system that baked Europe also sat over southern Louisiana for months, worsening a historic drought and wildfires, and later helped create a blinding 'super fog' tied to a 158-car highway pile-up that killed seven people. Researchers say these sprawling, slow-moving heat systems connect disasters that once looked unrelated.

For Ohio readers, the takeaway is practical: extreme heat is increasingly a systems problem, hitting power grids, roads, schools and health at the same time.

items.title: South Korea's central bank is expected to hold rates Thursday, then hike in November
items.summary:
The Bank of Korea will keep its key policy rate unchanged at 3.00% on Thursday after two consecutive increases, according to all 34 economists in a Reuters poll conducted October 14 to 19. The same poll expects one more increase next month.

Inflation eased to 2.9% in September from 3.1% in August but remains above the bank's 2% target. Strong semiconductor-led growth, recovering domestic demand and elevated energy costs are expected to keep underlying price pressure firm.

Governor Shin Hyun Song has called for time to assess the back-to-back hikes already delivered, giving policymakers room to pause rather than deliver a third straight increase. Economists at BNP Paribas say the pause does not mean the tightening cycle is over, with risks still tilted toward higher prices.

Korea's decision is a useful signal for the wider region, where chip-driven growth is running hot even as central banks try to finish the inflation fight.

items.title: House Republicans quietly scale back hopes for a big redistricting boost
items.summary:
House Republicans are quietly lowering expectations for the nationwide redistricting fight, Axios reports. Strategists who once talked about a 10-seat boost now privately worry, on their down days, that the whole effort could net the party only about one seat nationwide.

Two things changed the math: a souring political climate heading into the midterms, and polling showing a collapse in Republican support among Latino voters in Texas and Florida, two states that were supposed to anchor the gains.

Redistricting was meant to insulate the House majority before a single vote was cast. If the maps deliver only a seat or so, control of the House goes back to being decided the old-fashioned way, district by district, in a difficult environment for the party in power.

Watch the remaining state map fights and whether Latino polling moves again before Election Day, two weeks from today.

items.title: Defense Secretary Hegseth met Netanyahu in an unannounced visit to Israel, Axios reports
items.summary:
U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth met Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu during an unannounced visit to Israel on Monday, Axios reported, citing two sources with knowledge of the trip. Reuters said it could not immediately confirm the meeting, and the Pentagon and Israel's embassy in Washington did not immediately comment.

Hegseth said in a social media post that he had visited U.S. service members in the Central Command area, which covers the Middle East. Axios reported the talks came amid U.S.-Israeli discussions about potentially resuming major combat operations against Iran.

The visit landed one day after President Trump endorsed Netanyahu in next week's Israeli parliamentary election, the first since the October 7, 2023 Hamas attack. Polls suggest Netanyahu's coalition could lose its majority while the opposition may also struggle to form a government.

Watch for any official readout from either government, and for whether the Iran question becomes public before Israelis vote on October 27.

items.title: Vance declines to endorse Netanyahu while Trump gives him a 'complete and total' backing
items.summary:
Vice President JD Vance declined Monday to endorse Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for reelection, a day after President Trump gave him a full-throated endorsement ahead of Israel's October 27 election. Vance said he endorses American candidates and is focused on the November 3 U.S. midterms.

Trump praised Netanyahu on social media as a great warrior prime minister and a partner in confronting Iran, adding that without him the United States might have to finish the fight against Tehran on its own. Netanyahu thanked him, writing that together they would complete the mission.

The split is notable because Vance traveled to Budapest earlier this year and endorsed Hungary's Viktor Orban in his election, which Orban lost. His refusal this time reads as a deliberate choice to keep distance from a foreign race where the outcome is genuinely uncertain.

Polls suggest Netanyahu's religious-nationalist coalition could fall short of a majority, and the opposition may struggle to assemble one either.

items.title: Kennedy Center donation that allegedly vanished puts Ric Grenell under White House scrutiny
items.summary:
The White House counsel's office is investigating former Kennedy Center executive director Ric Grenell over an alleged $5.6 million donation that was never deposited, the New York Post reports. Alina Habba told President Trump in an October 9 Oval Office meeting that her husband, Turkish billionaire Turhan Mildon, was duped into providing the funds.

Texts first reported by Axios allegedly show Grenell promising Mildon access to administration events and the president himself once the money moved. Mildon provided records of a $17.6 million wire to a Texas defense software company, though Axios reported the money actually came from the Democratic Republic of Congo's finance ministry.

Grenell reportedly denied sending the key text, pointing to its British spelling of 'Centre.' He did not respond to the Post's request for comment. The allegations remain unproven, and no charges have been announced.

This is a story to treat carefully: it is an active White House investigation built on contested texts and an unusual money trail, and what can be documented will matter more than the claims.

items.title: Rubio, in Central Asia, says Ukraine and Russia should focus on ending the war
items.summary:
Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters during a visit to Uzbekistan on Monday that Ukraine and Russia should be focused on ending their war. Rubio landed in Samarkand Sunday night to meet officials of the C5+1 grouping of the United States and five Central Asian nations.

Asked about a possible meeting of Presidents Trump, Putin and Xi to negotiate an end to the conflict, Rubio said talks of a meeting exist but nothing is finalized, and that the president has been clear he wants the war ended. He warned of a real risk the war spreads if a sabotage attack or a drone knocked off course wanders into a neighboring country.

The U.S. has been mediating while also clinching a diesel import deal with Russia and waiving some sanctions on Moscow, moves Trump says keep the Kremlin at the table and that Kyiv has criticized.

Rubio's trip also underlines Washington's courtship of Central Asia, a region where Russia and China both compete for influence and where Trump hosted leaders at the White House last November.

items.title: Anthropic and Nscale are reportedly in talks for a second $45 billion compute deal
items.summary:
Barely a month after announcing a $45 billion computing agreement, Anthropic and infrastructure provider Nscale are reportedly close to a second deal of the same size, Bloomberg reports via TechCrunch. Sources cautioned the talks are still underway and the details could change.

Reporting on Nscale's planned IPO puts the first agreement at about $44.6 billion and links the possible second facility to its Monarch data center campus in West Virginia, at roughly 460 megawatts of capacity. Neither company confirmed the specifics to TechCrunch.

The scale is the story. Frontier AI labs are locking down power and chips years ahead, and some investors worry the industry is spending far more on infrastructure than current revenue justifies. Both Anthropic and Nscale are pursuing public listings, and Nscale is reportedly facing pushback over a proposed $30 billion valuation.

Watch for a formal announcement, and for whether IPO investors treat another mega-deal as confidence or as leverage piling up.

items.title: Blackwall raises $100 million at a $2.2 billion valuation to filter bot and AI traffic
items.summary:
Estonia-based Blackwall said Tuesday it has raised $100 million in a Series C round at a $2.2 billion valuation, quadrupling its value since its previous raise in 2025. The round was led by AVP, with Dawn Capital, MMC Ventures and Tera Ventures taking part.

Blackwall builds tools that help websites sort real visitors and legitimate automated traffic from malicious bots, scraping and DDoS attacks, a problem getting harder as AI agents crawl the web. Instead of selling directly to site owners, it sells white-label bundles through hosting, cloud and managed-service providers, which rebrand the tools for their own customers.

That channel model is its bet against giants like Cloudflare and Akamai: the host is often the only practical route to millions of smaller websites. The company says the new money will fund global expansion and a deeper platform.

As more of the internet's traffic becomes machines talking to machines, deciding which machines to let in is becoming a business of its own.

items.title: Japan's chip revival is being pulled into building America's semiconductor capacity instead
items.summary:
Japan will invest up to $21 billion to build two chip factories in New York state under a deal announced last week by GlobalFoundries, part of Tokyo's $550 billion U.S. investment pledge made with the Trump administration in return for lower tariffs. Under that deal, the U.S. president, not Japan, selects the projects.

That creates a tension at the heart of Japan's own semiconductor revival. Tokyo wants to rebuild domestic capability and supply-chain resilience, but experts say funding American plants does little for either, however much it buys goodwill in Washington.

A Japanese government source described investment in the U.S. as ultimately a measure for dealing with Trump, essentially buying time to maintain the relationship. The dynamic has history: in the 1980s, a dominant Japan agreed to restrict chip exports to the U.S., a period officials in Tokyo still remember bitterly.

South Korea and Taiwan have made similar pledges, so Japan is not alone in trading investment for tariff relief and security ties.

items.title: Cleveland-Cliffs swings back to profit and targets more than $4 billion in 2027 earnings
items.summary:
Cleveland-Cliffs reported a return to quarterly profitability on October 19, with third-quarter revenue rising to $5.61 billion from $4.73 billion a year earlier and adjusted EBITDA reaching $612 million. Management guided to about $715 million for the fourth quarter and more than $4 billion for 2027.

The steelmaker posted GAAP net income of $165 million, against a net loss of $234 million in the same quarter of 2025, with adjusted earnings of $0.28 per share. Executives credited better selling prices, volumes and operating costs after a difficult stretch of pricing pressure.

Separately, CEO Lourenco Goncalves used the earnings call to blame Canada's government for planned layoffs at Stelco in Ontario, saying Canada's galvanized steel market cannot support domestic producers plus an avalanche of imports under the current tariff-rate quota system. Cliffs temporarily laid off up to 500 Stelco workers in late September.

For Northeast Ohio, Cliffs remains a bellwether: the 2027 target assumes domestic steel prices and newly negotiated customer contracts hold up.

items.title: Broadcom rolls out VMware HyperArmor as its market value sits near $1.6 trillion
items.summary:
Broadcom has introduced VMware HyperArmor, a new security offering for its VMware platform, as the company's market capitalization stands around $1.6 trillion as of October 19. The launch lands while Broadcom's fiscal third-quarter figures point to unusually rapid growth in its AI business.

Market reporting cited in the coverage put third-quarter revenue at $29.6 billion, up sharply year over year, and noted Goldman Sachs raised its price target to $540 in September. Broadcom's next earnings date is December 9.

The valuation is the tension. Investors are paying for Broadcom to convert intense AI demand and new VMware products into the fourth-quarter revenue it has guided to, which leaves little room for an execution slip in either chips or software.

Watch the December earnings for whether AI orders and VMware renewals both keep pace with the price the market has already set.

items.title: Justice Department charges 28 people in California with voting crimes
items.summary:
The Justice Department announced Monday it is charging 28 noncitizens in California, all described as green card holders, with illegally registering to vote or voting in U.S. elections, NPR reported in its morning brief. Eleven people were arrested Monday, and the charges are accusations; defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty.

The department also filed an emergency court request to stop California from processing ballots from voters the federal government calls likely noncitizens. California officials say they asked how the federal government reached those conclusions and have not received the specifics.

Noncitizen voting has never been found to be widespread in American elections, but the administration is devoting significant resources to the cases it does find, announcing new charges in batches as early voting runs. Critics in California call the timing a political stunt tied to a state voter ID ballot measure.

With Election Day two weeks away, expect the court fight over California's ballots to move faster than the criminal cases.

items.title: U.S. orders DeepSeek AI removed from most civilian government systems
items.summary:
The United States has ordered civilian government agencies to remove DeepSeek's artificial intelligence technology from their systems, citing privacy and security risks including potential transfers of sensitive data to China. The Department of Homeland Security made the order public on October 19, though the ban took effect at the end of July.

The order covers agencies including the Treasury, State and Justice departments, and it also reaches technology built using DeepSeek's AI models. Agencies under the Department of Defense are excluded from this order.

The move is the latest step in Washington's effort to wall Chinese AI tools out of federal systems, treating model access as a data-security question rather than just a software choice. For vendors, it means provenance of the underlying model now matters in government contracts.

Watch for whether the exclusion expands to contractors and state governments, as earlier Chinese technology bans eventually did.

items.title: Trump says the U.S. and Mexico are close to a 'great' trade deal
items.summary:
President Trump said Monday in Kansas that the United States and Mexico are very close to agreeing to a trade deal he described as great. He made the remark at a political rally in Park City, Kansas, Reuters reported.

No terms were announced at the rally, and the brief report carried no Mexican government response. Mexico is one of America's largest trading partners, and any agreement would touch autos, agriculture and the supply chains that run through Ohio manufacturing.

Trade announcements at rallies have a history of preceding the paperwork by days or weeks, so the substance will be in the text: tariff levels, rules of origin and enforcement, none of which are public yet.

Watch for a formal statement from either government confirming what has actually been agreed.

items.title: Angel Reese's 30 points and 16 rebounds pull the Dream even in the WNBA Finals
items.summary:
Angel Reese had 30 points and 16 rebounds on Monday night as the Atlanta Dream beat the Golden State Valkyries 79-65 in San Francisco to even the best-of-seven WNBA Finals at one game apiece. Allisha Gray added 18 points, and Rhyne Howard set a Finals record with six steals.

It was Atlanta's first Finals victory after going winless in three previous trips. Reese became only the third player with at least 30 points and 15 rebounds in a Finals game, joining Jonquel Jones and Breanna Stewart, and at 24 the youngest with a 20-point double-double in Finals history.

Golden State shot just 34.4% and never recovered after halftime. The Valkyries, playing in front of another sellout at Chase Center, got 14 points each from Gabby Williams and Tiffany Hayes.

The series shifts to Atlanta for Game 3 on Wednesday, moved to the Hawks' larger State Farm Arena to fit the bigger crowd.

items.title: U.S. warns Americans across the Middle East about possible airspace closures
items.summary:
The United States issued security alerts on October 18 warning Americans across the Middle East about possible flight cancellations, airspace closures and rapidly escalating hostilities, according to an AP news summary. The warnings cover Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Kuwait, Jordan, Bahrain, Oman, Iran, Qatar, Iraq, Lebanon, Yemen and Israel.

The alerts arrived as Washington's posture in the region grew more entangled: the president endorsed Israel's prime minister for reelection, the defense secretary made an unannounced trip to Israel, and Egypt's top security body agreed to help Saudi Arabia defend itself against Houthi attacks while its parliament delayed a vote on military support.

For travelers, the practical meaning is simple: itineraries through Gulf and Israeli airspace can change with little notice, and Americans in the region are being told to monitor local conditions and embassy guidance closely.

Watch airline schedules and State Department updates; airspace warnings like these usually precede, not follow, disruptions.

items.title: Guardians' season ends in St. Petersburg: Rays win Game 6, 7-3, and the ALCS, 4-2
items.summary:
The Guardians' run ended Monday night at Tropicana Field, where Tampa Bay won Game 6 of the ALCS 7-3 to take the series four games to two. Cleveland opened with Shawn Armstrong and a bullpen plan that unraveled by the second inning, while Freddy Peralta held the Guardians to one run over 5 1/3 innings and was named series MVP.

Junior Caminero hit a two-run homer off the left-field foul pole in the seventh. Cleveland's one real swing came in the eighth, when a bases-loaded walk and a hit batter cut it to 5-3, but Kevin Kelly struck out Brayan Rocchio to end the threat, and former Guardian Yandy Diaz answered with a two-run homer in the bottom half.

It closes a year that included a 2-1 series lead in this ALCS and, earlier, a comeback from 0-2 down against the White Sox that only 11 of 96 teams have ever managed. The Rays now meet Milwaukee in the World Series starting Friday; two franchises with zero titles, and one of them finally gets one.

For Cleveland, the winter questions start immediately, beginning with an offense that disappeared at the wrong time and a roster built to contend again in 2027.

items.title: Nestlé will close its Solon factory by the end of 2027 and move production to South Carolina
items.summary:
Nestlé USA told employees Monday it plans to close its Solon factory by the end of 2027, moving its Nestlé Professional Solutions frozen meal pouch production to its plant in Gaffney, South Carolina. Production in Solon is set to wind down by the third quarter of next year, with the shutdown in the final quarter of 2027.

The decision affects only the factory, not Nestlé's Solon campus or its West 25th Street plant in Cleveland, and the company has not said exactly how many jobs are affected; local reporting put the figure in the hundreds. Impacted employees are being offered separation and transition support and can apply for open roles at other Nestlé sites, including in Ohio.

The roots here run deep: Stouffer's built the Solon plant in 1968 and sold to Nestlé in 1973, and brands like Lean Cuisine and DiGiorno have been managed from Solon since. Mayor Edward Kraus called it difficult news and said the city will work with state and regional partners on job placement for affected workers.

This is the biggest local business story of the week for Solon, and the one to watch for follow-through on worker support.

items.title: Ohio's secretary of state race is a referendum on how elections should run
items.summary:
Republican Robert Sprague and Democrat Allison Russo offer sharply different views of Ohio elections in the race for secretary of state, Signal Ohio reports. The two disagree on the state's voter ID law, drop boxes, redistricting and how much election fraud is actually happening.

Sprague, finishing his second term as state treasurer, has backed upfront citizenship checks at registration and has reconsidered his earlier support for making Election Day a state holiday. Russo, a state representative, argues that if there were massive fraud it would have happened on Republicans' watch, since they run Ohio's elections now.

There is no debate scheduled, and each campaign blames the other for that. Sprague also called his 2011 vote for the anti-union Senate Bill 5 a mistake, a small sign of how Ohio Republican politics on labor have shifted.

The winner takes a seat on the Ohio Redistricting Commission and the Ballot Board, so this down-ballot race shapes maps and ballot language for years.

items.title: Cleveland Public Power wants to restructure rates, with summer bills rising about $7 to $8 a month
items.summary:
Cleveland Public Power is proposing to restructure its electric rates and raise them over the next three years, in legislation introduced in City Council in September that council has not yet approved. If passed, the new rates start next year and step up again in 2028 and 2029.

The new design charges residential customers a flat monthly fee plus three usage tiers: one rate for the first 250 kilowatt-hours, a higher rate for the next 250, and a higher rate still above 500. The current system has two tiers split at 1,000 kilowatt-hours.

CPP has not published a typical-customer cost, but Signal's estimate puts winter bills up only a dollar or so while summer bills, when usage climbs, rise roughly $7 to $8 a month. Commissioner Ammon Danielson has said plainly that the utility needs upgrades and ratepayers ultimately bear those costs.

Council's decision will land in the middle of what Mayor Justin Bibb himself calls a cost-of-living crisis, which is why the vote is worth watching.

items.title: Cleveland City Council set to extend its data center moratorium into early 2027
items.summary:
Cleveland will likely take no new data centers at all in 2026. Legislation introduced Monday would extend the city's current pause, which was set to expire October 20, until January 29, 2027, while council finishes writing permanent rules.

Councilman Brian Kazy's Data Center Working Group studied laws across the country and heard hundreds of questions at three town halls. Residents, he said, want clear guidance on zoning, power grid strain and water usage before the AI building boom arrives in force.

Ohio already has 80 data centers operating and 189 planned, most clustered around Columbus, and about 125 Ohio communities had moratoriums as of September, including North Royalton, Kent and Grove City. A statehouse committee is working on statewide policy that will eventually shape House Bill 646.

For a city that wants the investment but fears the electricity bills, the extension buys time; the real decision is the permanent ordinance that follows.

items.title: Obama's October 24 Cleveland rally makes Cuyahoga County the center of Ohio's fall races
items.summary:
Former President Barack Obama will host a joint rally in Cleveland on October 24 with Dr. Amy Acton, the Democratic nominee for governor, and former Senator Sherrod Brown, who is running for Senate again. A Columbus Dispatch column argues the visit is the clearest signal of how badly Democrats want to win Ohio's two biggest races.

Acton's opponent is Vivek Ramaswamy, who has poured more than $36 million of his own money into the race and has campaigned with President Trump, most recently in Youngstown on October 12. Brown faces appointed Senator Jon Husted. Recent polling cited in market coverage shows Acton with narrow, consistent leads in most surveys.

The Cleveland logic is turnout. Cuyahoga County cast 667,000 ballots when Obama first carried Ohio in 2008 and 582,000 in 2024, and Ohio history is full of statewide races decided by the county's margin, from Truman in 1948 to Carter in 1976.

Saturday's crowd size, and whether it converts into early votes in the county, is the measurable to watch.

baby.fact: By late pregnancy your baby can already recognize familiar voices and even the rhythm of songs and stories heard often — newborns turn toward their parents' voices in the first days because they've been listening for months.
baby.fun: Tiny mission for today: pick one song to be 'the song' — the one you both sing or play on the drive home from the hospital — and play it once tonight so it's already a familiar sound.
